item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The question of how it looks like when not observed isn't moot, and should be easily answered by taking a photo of it while unobserved, since photos do not carry the change.

In the end, it seems like a very weak article even for the time, and the only thing going for it is a trick with a photo. Other articles did similar tricks, like the entity that only manifests through a story, but they are far more interesting as concepts instead of an excuse for random creepy images supposedly about my own subconscious.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The description of the rules governing the image on the photo is frustratingly unclear. It sounds like photographing the photo shows what the image is when the photo is unobserved: the same as it was the last time it was observed, or maybe just a blank box. But then it's said that the question of what is shown when the photo is unobserved is "moot". That is unnecessarily confusing. Anyway, ALL appearances, of anything, are undefined when the things in question are not being (even indirectly) observed. To point this out as being a special feature of this photo's image is silly and misleading.

Also, what happens when multiple people are already viewing it at a time when it wants to change its image? This is an obvious thing to test, and it's very strange that the article doesn't even mention it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Moot isn't slang. It's a formal term derived from Old English that sees quite a bit of use in arenas like philosophy and legal writings- means basically the same thing as "trivial" but with the added nuance that "even if it did have some sort of significance, we can't answer the question anyway".
